opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd approach it is to start from examples rather than from axioms. The thing we're trying to capture is this very familiar style of reasoning that mathematicians and physicists use all the time but don't really have a formal account of. You look at some quantity, say whether there are infinitely many twin primes, and you say, "Well, if I treat the events 'n is prime' and 'n+2 is prime' as roughly independent, with the obvious corrections for small divisors, I get this estimate." That estimate turns out to be extremely accurate, even though nobody can prove it. So there's clearly some kind of valid reasoning going on there, and the question is what the rules are.

So concretely, what I'd recommend is building up a big collection of cases where informal heuristic arguments work, and especially cases where they fail or need to be corrected, and then trying to write down a formal system that gets those cases right. The key feature you want is something like: by default you assume things are independent, so the expected value of a product is the product of the expected values, and then when someone points out a structural reason they're not independent, you update. Then the defeasibility is the whole point. You're not proving anything; you're making a best guess that can be revised when you notice more structure.

The hard part, and where most of the work goes, is avoiding inconsistency. It's really easy to write down rules where if you apply the presumption of independence in two different orders, or to two different decompositions of the same quantity, you get contradictory answers. And then the system can be exploited: you can argue for basically anything by choosing which things to treat as independent. So a big chunk of the research is finding the right notion of what an "argument" is and what it means to "account for" a correlation, such that adding more considerations reliably gets you closer to the truth rather than letting you cherry-pick.

I'd also say it helps a lot to work in very simple settings first. Things like boolean circuits, or small neural networks, or simple polynomial identities, where you can actually compute the ground truth and check whether your heuristic estimator is behaving sensibly. You want to ask: if I give the estimator some explanation of why the output of this circuit is biased, does it update in the right way? Does it avoid getting fooled? And you can get a lot of traction just by finding counterexamples to candidate definitions. Honestly, much of our progress has looked like proposing a definition, someone finding a weird case that breaks it, and then iterating.

And the reason I care about this, in the AI context, is that if we had a good formalization, we could use it to say something like: "here's an explanation for why this model behaves well on the training distribution," and then check whether that same explanation still applies on a new input, or whether the model is doing something for a different reason. That's a kind of mechanistic anomaly detection. So I'd also keep that application in mind as a guide. It tells you which properties actually matter, so you don't get lost trying to solve every philosophical problem about probability over logical statements, which is a very deep rabbit hole.

r001.rationale: The response recommends collecting informal heuristic arguments and developing a formal system that gets those cases right, including defining what counts as an argument and how an estimator should account for correlations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I'd frame the problem first, because I think the framing matters a lot for how you attack it. The presumption of independence is this thing mathematicians and physicists do all the time where you have some quantity you can't compute exactly, and you say "well, absent any reason to think these things are correlated, let's treat them as independent and see what we get." Primes behave like they're random, so you get heuristic estimates for twin primes. You assume a hard function is basically uncorrelated with some structured function and estimate an average. And the striking thing is that these arguments are usually right, and when they're wrong there's usually some identifiable reason, some structure you missed.

So the research question is: can you turn that into something formal? Not a proof system, because the conclusions aren't theorems, they're defeasible. Something more like a system where you make an estimate, and someone else can come along and point out a correlation you ignored, and then you have to revise. The thing we were trying to pin down is what the rules of that game should be.

The approach I'd actually recommend is to start from desiderata rather than from a mechanism. Write down what properties a good heuristic estimator should have. The obvious one is consistency with deduction, so if you can actually prove something, your estimate should agree with it. Then there's something like linearity, where your estimate of a sum is the sum of the estimates. And then the interesting one, which is the thing that captures the presumption of independence itself: if you have two quantities and you haven't been given any argument relating them, you should estimate their product as the product of their estimates. That's the default, and arguments are the thing that move you off the default.

And once you've written down properties like that, the research mostly becomes a search for counterexamples. You propose an estimator, you try to find a case where it does something obviously stupid, you patch it, you repeat. That's genuinely how we spent most of our time, and I think it's the right mode. It's much more like trying to find the right definition in math than like engineering a system.

The second piece of advice is to work with toy settings that are as small as possible while still having the relevant structure. So you don't start with the Riemann hypothesis. You start with things like: here's a boolean circuit, estimate the probability it outputs one on a random input. Or here are some polynomial identities over a finite field, estimate how often they hold. Those are rich enough that independence assumptions fail in interesting ways, but you can actually run things and check whether your estimator's behavior is sane.

And I'll say what I think the hard part is, because it's not the one people expect. People expect the hard part to be making the estimates good, like getting close to the truth. But actually the hard part is making the estimates coherent under the addition of arguments. You want a system where learning more never makes you look stupid in retrospect in a way you could have anticipated. There's a kind of no-Dutch-book flavor to it, like logical induction, but in a setting where you care about individual estimates rather than limiting behavior, and where you need it to be efficient. Getting all three of those at once, coherence, defeasibility, and tractability, is where every candidate we tried eventually broke.

The last thing I'd say is to keep in view why you care, which for me is alignment. The hope is that if you have a formal notion of heuristic argument, you could ask a model to explain why it believes its own outputs will be good, in a way that's checkable but doesn't require a full proof. So when you're evaluating candidate systems, it's worth asking not just "is this mathematically nice" but "could a neural network in principle produce arguments in this format about its own behavior." That constraint prunes a lot of otherwise appealing directions.

r001.rationale: The response frames the task as designing a coherent heuristic estimator with desiderata and rules for revising estimates. It does not clearly say that formalization means specifying what an estimator captures from a set of informal arguments.

astra-6.text:
I would start by looking at very simple cases where we think we know what the right reasoning looks like, and trying to understand what would justify that reasoning. I wouldn’t start by trying to write down a general axiom saying, “If you don’t know how two things are related, assume they’re independent.” That’s going to depend on how you represent the things, and it’s very easy to get inconsistent answers.

For example, suppose you have a sum of a lot of terms, each of which is either plus one or minus one. You’d like to say that, absent some reason for the terms to line up, the sum should have roughly square-root-sized fluctuations. But these might be deterministic mathematical quantities. So what does that claim mean? Where is the probability coming from? And what counts as a reason to expect a correlation?

The approach I find most promising is to try to formalize the process of making a heuristic argument. You have some computational budget, you’ve noticed certain relationships, and you want an estimate that incorporates those relationships without inventing additional structure. Then, when someone supplies a new argument showing that two quantities are correlated, your estimate should change appropriately.

A central difficulty is that the same quantity can have many different descriptions. An independence assumption that looks natural in one description can look absurd in another. So I’d spend a lot of time on examples involving alternative descriptions, asking which consistency conditions we can reasonably demand and which are too computationally expensive.

The first milestone would be a restricted setting where we can give a precise account of what information the estimator has, what assumptions it’s making, and why those assumptions are useful. If we can get that to work on a handful of nontrivial mathematical examples, I think we’ll have learned much more than from proposing a very general principle that we don’t know how to apply.

r001.rationale: The response proposes formalizing how an estimator uses a computational budget and noticed relationships to incorporate heuristic arguments without adding unsupported structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by trying to formalize what counts as a reason to depart from independence. You can’t just say, “These two things are independent unless there’s a proof otherwise,” because everything you’re reasoning about might be a deterministic mathematical fact. In some sense, all the dependencies are already there. The question is which dependencies your reasoning process can recognize and use.

For example, suppose you have two complicated Boolean expressions and you want to estimate the probability that both are true. Treating them as independent might be a reasonable starting point. But if they share a subexpression, or one is the negation of the other, you want your procedure to notice that and adjust its estimate. And you want it to do that consistently across different ways of writing the same problem.

So the research program I’d be excited about is: take a very restricted language of computations, specify a restricted class of arguments that can explain correlations, and ask whether you can construct an estimator that incorporates those arguments while otherwise making an independence assumption. Then gradually make the language and the arguments more expressive.

The hard part is getting those local explanations to fit together. You don’t want your answer to depend arbitrarily on which intermediate quantities you introduced, or to count the same evidence twice. I think even a toy setting where you could state those requirements precisely and satisfy them would be meaningful progress. I’d much rather have that than a very general definition where we don’t know whether it captures the examples we care about.

r001.rationale: The response proposes specifying a class of arguments that explain correlations and constructing an estimator that incorporates those arguments while otherwise assuming independence.
